qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture twelve. Virtualisation and containers. How to ship the whole kitchen along with the recipe.
Mo's forecaster, forecast dot py, is the same file on both machines.
Mo's forecaster: forecast.py, the same file on both machines.
But the laptop runs Windows eleven and Python three point twelve. The server runs Ubuntu and Python three point eight.

It runs on the laptop and crashes on the server.
The code is fine. The environment differs: the operating system, the libraries, the dependencies and the settings.
The environment differs: OS, libraries, dependencies, settings.
Code moves from development, to a test box, to the live production server.
Development, test, production: three machines that start out alike.
Each machine gets its own updates and tweaks.
Each gets its own updates and tweaks.
Slowly they drift apart, and moving code between them becomes fragile.
They drift apart, so deploying across them is fragile.
So here is the big idea. Pack the whole environment along with the code.
The big idea: pack the environment along with the code.
The real, physical computer is called the host.
The real computer is the host.
On it run virtual machines, called guests. Each has its own operating system and apps.
Each virtual machine is a guest with its own OS.
Underneath sits the hypervisor. It shares out the host's processor, memory and disk.
The hypervisor shares the host's CPU, memory and disk between them.
Popular hypervisors are VMware Workstation, VirtualBox and Hyper-V.
For example VMware Workstation, VirtualBox and Hyper-V.
An emulator pretends to be other hardware, like an old games console.
An emulator mimics other hardware, like an old console.
Every instruction is translated, so the game never touches the real hardware.
Every instruction is translated; the game never touches the real hardware.
A virtual machine is different. Its guest runs on the host's real hardware.
A virtual machine does use the host hardware.
The hypervisor just keeps the guests apart.
The hypervisor keeps the guests apart.
A snapshot saves the virtual machine's state at one exact moment.
A snapshot saves the VM's state at one exact moment.

Restore the snapshot: every later change is undone.
A snapshot can also be copied to another host.
Snapshots can also be copied to another host.
Here are three of Loafly's services, each in its own virtual machine.
Three services, three virtual machines.
Every virtual machine repeats a whole operating system. That is a lot of overhead.
Every VM repeats a whole OS: lots of overhead.
Containers share the host's kernel instead, and each brings only its libraries and its app.
Containers share the host's OS kernel instead.
In rough numbers, four operating systems against just one.
Rough numbers: 4 operating systems against 1.
So a container starts in milliseconds, while a virtual machine needs about a minute to boot.
A container starts in milliseconds, a VM in about a minute.
Docker packs the app with everything it needs: its Python, its libraries and its settings.
Docker packs the app with all its dependencies.
A container is an isolated process. Namespaces give it its own files, network and process list.
Namespaces: each container sees its own files, network and processes.
Cgroups set its budget: how much processor, memory and input and output it may use.
Cgroups: limits on CPU, memory and IO.
On a Windows laptop, Docker Desktop runs a small Linux virtual machine, through WSL two or Hyper-V.
On Windows, Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM via WSL2 or Hyper-V.
An image is a read-only template. One image can start three identical containers.
One image, three running containers.
A Dockerfile is the written recipe. Docker build runs it line by line, one layer per line.
A Dockerfile builds the image line by line, one layer each.
On the first build, every layer is made and cached.
First build: every layer is made and cached.
Change only your code, and just the last layer is rebuilt. Three come from the cache.
Change only your code: 1 layer rebuilt, 3 from cache.
Change the library list, and Docker rebuilds from that line down.
Change the library list: rebuilt from that line down.
Kubernetes runs a cluster: a control plane, the brain, above the worker nodes.
A cluster: a control plane and worker nodes.
A Deployment asks for three pods. A Service gives them one stable address.
A Deployment wants 3 pods; a Service gives them one address.
When a pod crashes, it is restarted.
A pod crashes: it is restarted.
When node two goes down, its pod is rescheduled. Three are running again, as desired.
Node 2 goes down: its pod is rescheduled. Still 3 running.
So you get scaling, self-healing, a declarative set-up, and support on every cloud.
Scaling, self-healing, declarative, cloud-native.
A virtual machine is a whole computer in software, run by a hypervisor.
A container shares the host's kernel, so it is light and quick to start.
A Dockerfile builds the image, and Kubernetes keeps the containers running as you asked.
